Azerbaijan Remembers 2016 General Strike That Brought the Country to a Standstill

Baku — This week marks eight years since the widespread general strike of 2016, a rare event in Azerbaijan’s modern history that halted economic activity nationwide for two days. While life has since returned to normal, many still recall the unprecedented scenes of closed shops, empty offices, and silent factories across Baku and the regions.

The strike, which began on March 14, 2016, was the result of coordinated action by multiple trade unions representing workers in transport, retail, and public services. The unions demanded urgent action to address rising inflation and wage stagnation following the sharp devaluation of the manat earlier that year.

“We had reached a breaking point,” said Kamal Huseynov, a former leader in the National Workers’ Confederation. “Prices were rising every week, but salaries stayed the same. People felt their voices were not being heard.”

The walkout saw bus and metro services in Baku suspended, offices across the energy and construction sectors deserted, and retail outlets shuttered in cities such as Ganja, Sumgayit, and Mingachevir. According to the Azerbaijan Chamber of Commerce, the two-day stoppage resulted in an estimated $120 million in lost economic output.

Government officials at the time called for calm and urged dialogue. “We recognize the hardships faced by our citizens and are committed to finding solutions,” then-Minister of Social Protection Rauf Mammadov stated on national television. Emergency talks between union leaders and government representatives eventually led to a temporary agreement on wage increases for key public sector employees, as well as a review of food price controls.

Economic analysts say the 2016 strike was a turning point. “It was a wake-up call for policymakers,” said Leyla Aliyeva, an economist at the Baku Policy Forum. “It forced the government to take immediate steps to stabilize the currency and introduce modest social support measures.”

In the years since, Azerbaijan has seen relative economic stability, though challenges remain. Unions are now less vocal, but many workers remember the solidarity of 2016. “We showed that ordinary people can make their voices heard,” said Ilkin Abbasov, who participated in the strike in Ganja.

As Azerbaijan looks ahead, the general strike of 2016 remains a reminder of both the vulnerabilities and the resilience of its workforce. No similar disruption has occurred since, but the lessons of that week continue to shape economic policy discussions.
